# OpenHikes repository instructions

## Build and test

The main project requires Xcode 26.5+, the iOS 26.5 platform, and a development team capable of signing the WeatherKit entitlement, the shared App Group, the iCloud container and the push entitlement. The shared package can be built and tested independently on macOS.

```sh
# Build the app and its embedded widget target
xcodebuild build \
  -project OpenHikes.xcodeproj \
  -scheme OpenHikes \
  -destination 'platform=iOS Simulator,name=iPhone 17 Pro'

# Run all app-hosted tests
xcodebuild test \
  -project OpenHikes.xcodeproj \
  -scheme OpenHikes \
  -destination 'platform=iOS Simulator,name=iPhone 17 Pro'

# Run one app test suite or one test method
xcodebuild test -project OpenHikes.xcodeproj -scheme OpenHikes \
  -destination 'platform=iOS Simulator,name=iPhone 17 Pro' \
  -only-testing:OpenHikesTests/HikeStatisticsTests
xcodebuild test -project OpenHikes.xcodeproj -scheme OpenHikes \
  -destination 'platform=iOS Simulator,name=iPhone 17 Pro' \
  -only-testing:OpenHikesTests/HikeStatisticsTests/elevationGainAndLoss\(\)

# Run just the widget bundle
xcodebuild test -project OpenHikes.xcodeproj -scheme OpenHikes \
  -destination 'platform=iOS Simulator,name=iPhone 17 Pro' \
  -only-testing:OpenWidgetTests

# Run simulator UI automation and launch performance metrics
xcodebuild test -project OpenHikes.xcodeproj -scheme OpenHikesUI \
  -destination 'platform=iOS Simulator,name=iPhone 17 Pro'

# Run the standalone shared-package suite
swift test --package-path OpenHikesShared

# Run one shared-package suite or test
swift test --package-path OpenHikesShared --filter MercatorTests
swift test --package-path OpenHikesShared \
  --filter 'OpenHikesSharedTests.MercatorTests/tileIndicesUnchanged'
```

Unit and integration tests use Swift Testing (`@Suite`, `@Test`, `#expect`). `-only-testing:` fails **silently** in two ways, both of which report a green run having executed nothing: an identifier it cannot resolve is ignored outright — which is what a suite declared inside an `extension` looks like, so `-only-testing:OpenHikesTests/BackgroundDeliveryTests` selects nothing because that suite lives in `extension WidgetFeedSuites` — and a Swift Testing *method* needs its trailing `()`, so `…/HikeStatisticsTests/elevationGainAndLoss` runs zero tests while `…/elevationGainAndLoss()` runs it. Neither produces a warning. Any job that pins a list of `-only-testing:` entries must therefore assert the resulting suite and test counts, as the `thread-sanitizer` job does. The `OpenHikesUITests` simulator bundle uses XCTest/XCUITest because Apple's UI automation and performance metrics are not available through Swift Testing. The main `xcodebuild test` action runs the two app-hosted bundles, `OpenHikesTests` and `OpenWidgetTests`, plus `OpenHikesUITests`; the dedicated `OpenHikesUI` scheme runs only UI automation. `OpenWidgetTests` compiles the `OpenWidget/` sources into itself, since an app extension cannot host a test bundle.

App tests use the in-memory SwiftData fixtures in `OpenHikesTests/General/TestSupport.swift`. A suite that touches the tile pipeline builds a `TileSandbox` — its own `TileCache` directories and its own `AutoSaveTileStore` — rather than `TileCache.shared`; the singletons belong to the app, and the whole bundle shares one process. Likewise `BackgroundTrailTracker`, `LocationManager` and `OfflineTileDownloader` take injectable location, defaults, clock and transport, so no test depends on wall-clock time, a real connection, or the host app's settings.

UI-test app launches pass `--ui-testing`, which selects an in-memory SwiftData store and isolated `UserDefaults`. Additional launch arguments can expand the sheet (`--ui-test-expanded-sheet`), enable real simulator Core Location (`--ui-test-enable-location`), import a bundled GPX fixture (`--ui-test-import-gpx=ThumseeLoopFast`), match against a bundled trail graph instead of Overpass (`--ui-test-trail-graph=ThumseeRidgePath`), give the tile cache its own empty storage root and no network monitor so every tile is a genuine miss (`--ui-test-offline`), seed a hike with generated photos (`--ui-test-seed-photos=<count>`) or the field-metrics store with reports (`--ui-test-seed-metrics=<count>`), fail the first save of a finished recording so the retry path is reachable (`--ui-test-fail-first-save`), serve a fixed forecast instead of WeatherKit (`--ui-test-weather`), grant the paid-map entitlement without StoreKit (`--ui-test-entitled`), seed a fake photo library (`--ui-test-photo-library=<count>`), or open a performance log for a named scenario (`--ui-test-performance-log=<scenario>`). Every one of them is `DEBUG`-only and takes effect only alongside `--ui-testing`; `AppLaunchEnvironment` is the single source of truth for all of them, and a new one belongs there and in this list beside the rest. XCUITest drives static locations through `XCUIDevice.shared.location`; longer route playback remains available through `Scripts/simulate-hike.sh`. `Scripts/run-ui-tests.sh` boots one UI test (`--test`), one class (`--suite … --all`) or every functional class (`--all`) against a named simulator; `--list` prints them as `Class/method`. Fixtures, launch helpers and gestures shared by the bundle live in `OpenHikesUITests/UITestSupport.swift`, and the audit types, MapKit filter and report formatting in `OpenHikesUITests/AccessibilityAuditSupport.swift` — reuse them rather than re-deriving a coordinate or a wait. The bundle is split by subject, one class per file because SwiftLint's `single_test_class` requires it: `OpenHikesUITests` (map, sheet, hike details), `RecordingUITests`, `PhotoUITests`, `SettingsUITests`, `AccessibilityUITests`, `AccessibilityLabelUITests` and `PerformanceUITests`.

`PerformanceUITests` is a measurement suite rather than a correctness one. `--ui-test-performance-log=<scenario>` makes `PerformanceLog` write every signpost mark and interval, every `MainThreadWatchdog` stall and a 1 Hz CPU/footprint/power sample to `Documents/PerformanceLogs/<scenario>.tsv`; the test additionally sets `RENDER_SIGNPOST_LOG=1` in `launchEnvironment`, since a test plan's environment reaches the runner and not the app. Because the test is out of process, it reads live counters through the `performance-counters` accessibility probe. `Scripts/run-performance-tests.sh` runs the suite, pulls the TSVs with `simctl get_app_container`, and renders a report through `Scripts/perf-report.py`. Baseline numbers and the open work live in `PERFORMANCE.md`.

Two `xcodebuild test` runs cannot share a simulator. They install the same bundle identifier onto the same device, so the second install tears the first run's app out from under it, and the failure arrives as `Test crashed with signal kill` landing on whichever test happened to be executing — a different one each time, with no assertion and no diagnostic. Under load it also arrives as `kAXErrorServerNotFound`, `Application … is not running`, or a run that dies before any test starts. Four separate investigations this repository has run mistook that signature for a product bug, and one of them measured load average 101–180 while chasing it. If a run fails *differently* each time, or fails in an area nobody touched, suspect the device before the code: create a private device with `xcrun simctl create`, target it by UDID, and delete it afterwards. A green run on a contended simulator is no more trustworthy than a red one.

Neither the functional UI automation nor the performance suite runs in CI both drive a booted simulator through real gestures and timing-sensitive waits, which a shared runner makes slow and flaky, and the performance suite needs stable hardware for its numbers to mean anything. The accessibility classes are the exception: the `accessibility-ui-tests` job runs `AccessibilityUITests` and `AccessibilityLabelUITests` through `Scripts/run-ui-tests.sh --suite <class> --all --retry`, granting location with `simctl privacy` up front so the two location-dependent tests never see a permission alert. That job is `continue-on-error: true` until its flake rate is known, so a red run reports without blocking. `PerformanceUITests` is listed in `skippedTests` for `OpenHikes.xctestplan`, so `xcodebuild test -scheme OpenHikes` does not pay for it; the `OpenHikesUI` scheme autocreates its plan and therefore still sees it, which is how `Scripts/run-performance-tests.sh` selects it. `Scripts/run-ui-tests.sh` names its functional classes explicitly — today `OpenHikesUITests`, `RecordingUITests`, `PhotoUITests`, `SettingsUITests`, `AccessibilityUITests` and `AccessibilityLabelUITests` — for the same reason, so a new class has to be added to that list to be reachable through the script, and its `measurement_tests` list keeps `testLaunchPerformance` out of `--all` while still allowing `--test testLaunchPerformance`. A new UI test class added to that bundle inherits none of this and must be placed on the correct side of it.

Three things that suite learned the hard way. Absolute memory readings taken under XCUITest are automation overhead, not the app's footprint — the same build launched by `simctl` sits substantially lower, and `PERFORMANCE.md` carries the current pair of numbers — so only compare footprints within a run. The first hit-test against a newly presented screen makes SwiftUI evaluate bodies, so a phase must warm the accessibility tree before it starts counting or it is charged for the previous screen. And `stopMeasuring()` truncates `XCTApplicationLaunchMetric`'s signpost interval, which makes `harvestData` raise rather than report; let the measure block end on its own.

A UI test that spoofs a route has to respect `RecordingFixPolicy`: a static simulated location is delivered once, so a fix rejected for implied speed or displacement has to be set again, and the test waits on the `recording-point-count` element rather than on a fixed sleep. Accessibility identifiers belong on the leaf views automation taps — SwiftUI pushes a container's identifier down onto every descendant, which would leave a whole screen answering to one name.

A suite that genuinely cannot run without an environment capability (today: the App Group container) stays conditionally enabled, but must report the skip through `SuitePrecondition`; strict mode turns a missing precondition into a failure — `xcodebuild test … "SWIFT_ACTIVE_COMPILATION_CONDITIONS=\$(inherited) REQUIRE_ALL_SUITES"` from a command line, or `OPENHIKES_REQUIRE_ALL_SUITES=1` in the scheme's test action from Xcode (a simulator-hosted test bundle inherits nothing from the invoking shell, which is why there are two).

Lint with `Scripts/lint.sh` (`--fix` applies what SwiftLint can correct). It runs strict SwiftLint at the version pinned in `.swiftlint-version`, and the CI `quality` job invokes that same script, so local and CI results cannot drift. It exits 0 clean, **2** for violations found and **1** for "could not run" — the third case exists because a `.swiftlint.yml` that fails to parse is only a *warning* to SwiftLint, which then lints on against the default configuration and can report a clean run having read no config at all.

The Xcode build also lints, through SwiftLintPlugins' `SwiftLintBuildToolPlugin` attached to `OpenHikes`, `OpenWidgetExtension`, `OpenHikesTests` and `OpenWidgetTests`. It runs `swiftlint lint --quiet --force-exclude` — no `--strict`, and at the version the package resolves to rather than the one in `.swiftlint-version` — so every *warning*-severity violation is invisible to it, and `Scripts/lint.sh` is what a change has to pass. An *error*-severity violation is the opposite: the plugin is a **prebuild** command, SwiftLint exits 2, and the target fails before a single file is compiled, which takes `build-for-testing` down for all four targets at once. So the error-severity rules are not advisory, they are a build gate, and these are the thresholds a large file or a branchy function actually trips: `file_length` 900, `cyclomatic_complexity` 18, `type_body_length` 450, `function_body_length` 90, `closure_body_length` 80, `line_length` 160, `identifier_name` 2–70 characters, `function_parameter_count` 9, `large_tuple` 4, and — inherited from SwiftLint's defaults rather than named in `.swiftlint.yml` — `enum_case_associated_values_count` 6. Nine more are error on a *single* occurrence: `attribute_name_spacing`, `duplicate_conditions`, `duplicate_enum_cases`, `dynamic_inline`, `force_cast`, `force_try`, `invisible_character`, `shorthand_operator` and `unhandled_throwing_task`. None of this is visible in `.swiftlint.yml`, which contains no literal `severity: error` line.

What keeps a scratch copy of the tree out of the lint is `included:`, not `excluded:` — SwiftLint's directory walk does **not** skip dot-directories, so a git worktree or a plain copy at the repository root is lintable material. `included:` stops applying the moment an explicit path is passed on the command line, which is exactly how the plugin invokes it, so `excluded:` carries `"**/.*"` as the durable guard rather than the name of whichever scratch directory exists today. `Scripts/install-git-hooks.sh` installs an opt-in pre-push hook. There is no formatting command.

Three optional tools are used if installed and skipped if not; the README lists the `brew install` line. `xcbeautify` formats `xcodebuild` output, and `Scripts/lib/xcodebuild-output.sh` is the one place that decides how — both UI scripts source it, and it falls back to their previous `grep` filter on a machine without it. Its constraint is load-bearing and is why those scripts still keep a raw log: xcbeautify prints nothing at all for output it cannot parse, which covers `measured [...]` lines, indented `PERF-` markers, ThreadSanitizer race reports, and any test failure with no recognised diagnostic — a crash or a hang produces no formatted line, not even `** TEST FAILED **`. It understands Swift Testing, so a failing `@Test` keeps its issue text and `file:line`. CI pipes every `xcodebuild` and `swift test` call through it under `--renderer github-actions` except the TSan job, whose raw report is the product; each of those `run:` blocks needs `set -o pipefail`, because Actions runs `bash -e` without it and would otherwise report the formatter's exit status rather than xcodebuild's. `periphery scan` reads `.periphery.yml` and reports unreferenced declarations; it is not in CI because it rebuilds the project with indexing enabled, and its report is candidates to read rather than a verdict — `--exclude-tests` finds the declarations only tests use, at the cost of listing every deliberate test seam alongside them. `xcode-build-server config -project OpenHikes.xcodeproj -scheme OpenHikes` regenerates `buildServer.json`, which is what lets `sourcekit-lsp` resolve symbols in the app target rather than only in the shared package; it holds absolute paths, so it is gitignored and is regenerated after adding or renaming a target.

That plugin only runs once its package fingerprint is trusted, and the trust lives per user in `~/Library/org.swift.swiftpm/security/plugins.json`, outside the repository — so a fresh CI machine fails with `Plugin "SwiftLintBuildToolPlugin" ... must be enabled before it can be used`. The checked-in `AllowedPackagePlugins.json` covers opening the project locally; CI does not read it. Every `xcodebuild` call in `.github/workflows/ci.yml` therefore passes `-skipPackagePluginValidation`, and a new one must too. Xcode Cloud composes its own `xcodebuild` invocation and cannot take that flag, so `ci_scripts/ci_post_clone.sh` — which Xcode Cloud runs by name after cloning — sets `IDESkipPackagePluginFingerprintValidatation` (Apple's typo, not ours) and `IDESkipMacroFingerprintValidation` instead. Adding a package that ships a build tool plugin or a macro needs no further change; removing the SwiftLint plugin would make all of it dead weight.

`AccessibilityUITests` and `AccessibilityLabelUITests` are the VoiceOver suites. The first sweeps `performAccessibilityAudit` per screen and the second asserts the labels, values and traits the app promises, because the audit cannot know that a provider row is the selected one or that the elevation graph should speak the point under the tracker. It runs with `.contrast`, `.textClipped` and `.dynamicType` subtracted — each exclusion is argued next to it, and `.dynamicType` in particular reports SwiftUI nodes it cannot introspect, including a navigation bar's own "Done" button. Issues whose detail names an `MK`-prefixed class are MapKit's and are filtered rather than fixed. Widening either exclusion needs the same argument; an audit that starts failing on a view the app does draw is a real regression.

A test that provokes a `nonisolated` delegate callback must wait through `settleDelegateHop(until:)` in `OpenHikesTests/General/SettleSupport.swift`, naming the effect it expects, rather than spinning a fixed number of `Task.yield()`s. A yield count buys an amount of progress that depends on machine load — which is how `Map coordinator` and `Location publishing` went red on CI while passing locally. Both unit bundles are `parallelizable: false` in `OpenHikes.xctestplan`, which is what makes those deadlines mean anything: the bundle is main-actor isolated project-wide, so Swift Testing's in-process parallelism could never run two tests at once, only interleave a thousand of them at their suspension points against one executor. Run 33049137656 is what that cost — seven recording tests starved together, and a five-second budget took seventeen seconds of wall time to notice it had expired. Serializing is the fix; a bigger budget is not. The condition-less overload is best-effort only, and a bare settle is almost always dead code now: because the delegate bodies deliver through `onMainActor`, a stub's `deliver(...)` runs the callback synchronously before it returns, so an assertion reading a synchronous effect (`stats`, `phase`, `trace`, a stub counter) needs no settle at all. Keep a *conditioned* settle wherever the effect is genuinely deferred — a journal flush, live matching, a shared widget snapshot, trail-graph prefetch state, the review preview, or `locationManagerDidChangeAuthorization`, which still hops explicitly because it awaits. The same rule bans a fixed `Task.sleep` as a barrier: wait on the positive effect that must follow, then assert the thing you are denying never happened.

## Architecture

- Following Apple's Food Truck and Backyard Birds samples, `OpenHikes/` is organized by product domain rather than generic `Managers`, `Models`, and `Views` layers. `App/` is the composition root; `Hikes/`, `Recording/`, `Map/`, `Tiles/`, `Photos/`, `Weather/`, `Purchases/`, `Sync/`, and `Settings/` own their related models, services, and views.
- `OpenHikesApp` creates one `OpenHikesModel` and injects it through the SwiftUI environment. That model owns the single `ModelContainer` plus long-lived location, weather, background tracking, auto-save, cloud sync, and recording dependencies; `OpenHikesView` owns transient selection, map presentation, and navigation state. `Hike` is the persisted source of truth, while `RouteProfile` is the precomputed distance/elevation index used by both chart scrubbing and GPS route matching. Stopping a recording that the matcher moved or found ambiguous ends in `.reviewing` rather than in the store: `RouteReviewSection.sections(in:)` groups the per-fix legs into reviewable sections, `RecordingRouteReview` holds the per-section `TrailRouteChoice`, and only `saveReviewedRecording()` writes the `Hike`.
- The map is an imperative MapKit subsystem behind `MapView`. `MapView.Coordinator` observes stable controller objects and updates `MKMapView` directly. Tile drawing flows through `CachingTileOverlayRenderer` and `TileOverlay` into `TileCache`; passive durable saves go through `AutoSaveTileStore`, while policy-permitted bulk downloads go through `OfflineTileDownloader`.
- `OpenHikesShared` is a local Swift package consumed by the app and iOS widget. Its source and tests mirror the `Recording/`, `Trails/`, `Widget/`, `LiveActivity/`, and `General/` domains; put cross-target payloads, projections, deep links, and shared presentation logic there rather than duplicating them in targets.
- The app precomputes a compact `SharedTrailSnapshot`, writes it atomically through `SharedStore`, and reloads widget timelines. The iOS widget reads that App Group store directly and does not recompute route matching or read location itself. Both `SharedTrailSnapshot` and `SharedRecordingSnapshot` carry an *optional* `schemaVersion`. Optional because synthesized `Decodable` throws rather than applying a property default for an absent key, so a non-optional field would have discarded every payload already on disk on the update that introduced versioning; an absent version means version 0 and is accepted if it decodes. `SharedStore` stamps the version on write rather than carrying it from the value, so a pre-versioning container upgrades itself on the first save instead of re-deciding the legacy question on every walk. A payload announcing a version newer than `currentSchemaVersion` is refused *before* decoding rather than half-accepted — a v2 payload may well still decode as v1, which is the dangerous case, since a re-meant field would be read with the old meaning. Every refusal, version mismatch or decode failure, is reported as a `SharedStoreDiagnostic` to the `OpenHikes`/`SharedStore` log with the offending key and coding path named; `os.Logger` rather than `RenderSignpost` because the package is consumed by an extension and `RenderSignpost` is app-target-only. Adding an optional key is still safe and needs no bump; renaming, retyping or removing a non-optional key still fails to decode and still blanks the widget, but now says why. `TrailBasemapSet` carries no version deliberately — it is regenerable derived state, so a schema change costs one render rather than a blank widget — but its decode failures are reported the same way, because an undecodable manifest re-renders forever.
- The Live Activity is split across all three targets along the same seam the widget is. `OpenHikesShared/LiveActivity/` owns `HikeActivityAttributes` — the payload — plus its content builders and `HikeActivityPresentation`, which decides every word, rounding and chip on both surfaces and is the testable half of the UI. `OpenWidget/` draws it. `OpenHikes/LiveActivity/` decides *when* one exists. The payload is a plain `Codable, Hashable, Sendable` struct and its `ActivityAttributes` conformance lives alone in `HikeActivityAttributes+ActivityKit.swift` behind `#if os(iOS)`: ActivityKit *is* importable on macOS, but `ActivityAttributes`, `Activity` and `ActivityContent` are all `@available(macOS, unavailable)`, so `canImport` is the wrong guard and the package's macOS support — which is what lets `swift test` run 181 tests on a Mac in CI — would otherwise have to go. The attributes *type name* is a storage contract: ActivityKit identifies a running activity by it, so renaming the type orphans every activity already on screen.
- A Live Activity never reads the App Group store, a location or a route profile; it renders `context.state` and nothing else, exactly as the widget renders its snapshot. Both surfaces are fed from the same two funnels the widget is fed from — `HikeRecorder.publishSharedRecordingSnapshot(force:)` and `BackgroundTrailTracker.updateStoredLiveFix` — so the two can only ever disagree about a *rate*, never about a fact. The polyline is deliberately left out of the payload: attributes plus `ContentState` share a 4 KB budget, and `payloadFitsTheActivityBudget` asserts it. `ContentState` carries `elapsedSeconds` and `updatedAt` so the view can derive a `timerStart` and hand the ticking to `Text(timerInterval:)`, which the system advances without spending an ActivityKit update; `RunState` is what says whether that timer may run, because a `Text(timerInterval:)` cannot be stopped once drawn.
- Target folders are Xcode file-system-synchronized groups. New Swift files under `OpenHikes/`, `OpenHikesTests/`, `OpenHikesUITests/`, `OpenWidget/`, or `OpenWidgetTests/` are discovered by their corresponding targets; place files in the target that should compile them. `OpenWidget/` is synchronized into two targets — the extension and `OpenWidgetTests` — with `OpenWidgetBundle.swift` excluded from the latter, since a test bundle must not carry a second `@main`.

## Repository-specific conventions

- Preserve render isolation. High-frequency GPS, sheet, chart-scrub, route-styling, and map-command state lives in stable `@Observable` reference types such as `RouteHighlight`, `SheetMetrics`, `RouteStyle`, `MapController`, `TrackerState`, and `LocationManager`. Parent SwiftUI bodies must not read their changing properties; `MapView.Coordinator` uses `withObservationTracking` to update only MapKit. Use `RenderSignpost` and the `RENDER_SIGNPOST_LOG=1` scheme variable when changing this flow.
- UI and SwiftData coordination are main-actor isolated. Delegate callbacks are `nonisolated` and reach that state through `onMainActor { ... }` in `General/MainActorDelivery.swift`, which runs the body synchronously via `MainActor.assumeIsolated` when the callback already arrived on the main thread and falls back to `Task { @MainActor in ... }` when it did not. Every `CLLocationManager` here is created on the main actor, so its deliveries take the synchronous path — which is what removes a heap allocation per GPS fix across three live delegates, and what restores ordering between consecutive batches, since two separate unstructured tasks on one actor have no defined order and a reordered pair is silently dropped by `RecordingFixPolicy`'s `interval > 0` guard. A callback that has to `await` (authorization changes, `withObservationTracking` re-arming) keeps the explicit `Task { @MainActor in ... }`; a `withObservationTracking` `onChange` **must** stay deferred, since it fires mid-mutation. Tile math, image encoding, disk enumeration, and other blocking pipeline work stay off the main thread; existing hot paths call `assertOffMainThread`. Keep shared off-main types `Sendable` and protect mutable singleton state with the existing lock pattern.
- Going the *other* way needs `Task.detached` or a `nonisolated` function, never a bare `Task {}`. A `Task {}` started from a method on a `@MainActor` type inherits that isolation and runs its body on the main thread, so any synchronous call inside it blocks the UI while looking exactly like offloaded work. This shipped once: `CloudSyncCoordinator` built its `CKContainer` inside such a task, and CloudKit's framework load and daemon handshake pinned the main thread for seconds on a fresh install — a grey map, no sheet, and an unresponsive app on a new user's first launch. `CloudSyncCoordinator.offMainThread(_:)` is the guarded seam and `CloudSyncCoordinatorTests` fails if either safeguard is removed. Making a property `lazy` does not help: it changes *when* the work runs, not *where*.
- Respect tile-provider policy. `TileProvider.supportsBulkDownload` gates prefetching: OpenStreetMap is passive auto-save only. Tile identity includes provider, zoom/x/y, and display scale. When deleting durable tiles, use `TileOwnership` so tiles shared by multiple hikes are not removed.
- Present modals from inside the sheet, not beside it. `OpenHikesView` keeps `MapSheet` presented permanently and puts it back if it is ever dismissed, so a `.sheet`, `.fullScreenCover`, `.photosPicker` or `.fileImporter` attached to the same view as that sheet is never presented at all — no error, just a button that does nothing. `MapSheet`'s `.fileImporter` and `.photoCapturePickers` are inside it for this reason; alerts are the exception and stay on the root view, where they survive the sheet being rebuilt.
- Files written outside SwiftData need an owner and a sweep. Photo and tile deletion is fire-and-forget, so termination can leave files with nothing pointing at them; `TileCache.trimCache(claimedBy:)` and `HikePhotoStore.reclaimOrphans(claimedBy:)` are the backstops, both driven at launch from a *complete* claim set — a fetch that fails must sweep nothing rather than sweep with an empty set.
- `TileCache` intentionally has memory, ephemeral cache, and durable Application Support tiers. Do not turn a render miss into synchronous disk/network work, and do not move expensive storage measurement into a SwiftUI body.
- The SwiftData store is not migrated across schema changes: a store written by an older shape of `Hike` is not a supported input, and a user whose store no longer opens reinstalls the app (losing their saved hikes and their durable tiles with it). CloudKit mirroring, however, does impose two rules that are checked at store-open time and easy to trip over later: every non-optional column on `Hike` must carry an inline declaration default, and uniqueness constraints are forbidden outright — which is why `Hike` and `HikeLocalState` both use `#Index` and neither uses `#Unique`.
- iCloud sync is SwiftData's own CloudKit mirroring, not a sync engine this repo owns. `Hike` lives in a store built with `cloudKitDatabase: .automatic`; everything describing files in *this* device's Application Support lives in `HikeLocalState`, a second `@Model` in a second, unmirrored `ModelConfiguration`. That split is load-bearing, not cosmetic: `TileOwnership` builds its claim set from `offlineDownloads` and `autoSavedTileKeys`, and `TileCache.trimCache(claimedBy:)` deletes whatever no hike claims, so mirroring those columns last-writer-wins would strip a second device of tiles it genuinely downloaded. `ModelConfiguration+OpenHikes.swift` is the only place `cloudKitDatabase` is named — build containers through its `ModelContainer.openHikes(...)` factories rather than with a `ModelConfiguration(` literal. Cross-store relationships are illegal, so the two rows join on `hikeID` by value and deleting a hike must call `hike.deleteLocalState()` by hand, *after* any tile-deletion plan has been built from the claim set it is about to remove. A new device-local column belongs in `HikeLocalState` with a passthrough on `Hike`; a new synced column belongs on `Hike` with an inline default. `CloudSyncCoordinator` only reports and toggles: it reads `NSPersistentCloudKitContainer.eventChangedNotification`, reduces each event to a `Sendable` `CloudSyncOutcome` on the posting thread, and surfaces `pendingRelaunch` because a `ModelConfiguration` cannot change its mind mid-launch.
- Remember only the *negative* entitlement answer. `MapEntitlementStore` persists its resolved answer under `SettingsKey.lastKnownMapEntitlement` and seeds `.notEntitled` at init when that answer was negative, but leaves state `.unknown` when it was positive. The asymmetry is the point: `.unknown` is already permissive, so a subscriber's map never flickers locked on a cold launch before StoreKit answers, while a non-subscriber is never served billed tiles in that window. Seeding the positive too would make a lapsed subscription paint an unlocked map until StoreKit disagreed. The store takes injectable `defaults`; `OpenHikesModel.entitlementDefaults(_:)` hands the app-hosted test bundles a wiped suite so a stub never writes into the developer's real defaults.
- **A recording always outranks a followed trail**, and one `HikeLiveActivityController` instance is what makes that expressible — the recorder and the tracker are handed the same object. A recording is the thing that would be *lost*; a follow is a convenience the walker can recreate by selecting the trail again. The controller also owns every rate decision: a 20-second update floor, a 10-second floor on the status flips that bypass it (pausing, losing the trail), stale dates of 10 minutes for a recording and 30 for a follow, and a 5-minute lingering final panel for a *finished* recording only. A discarded recording leaves nothing behind — `end(subject:finalState:dismissAfter:)` treats a `nil` final state as "take it off screen now", and substituting the current state there once silently defeated the discard path. A follow starts only on a *matched* fix, never on mere selection, but keeps updating on an unmatched one so "off the trail" can be said.
- There are no buttons on the Live Activity, and adding one is a larger change than it looks. A `LiveActivityIntent` runs in the *app's* process, so its type has to compile into both the app and the extension — and `OpenHikes/` and `OpenWidget/` are file-system-synchronized groups belonging to different targets, which leaves only the shared package, from which AppIntents metadata extraction is unproven here. The whole panel is a deep-link tap target reusing `TrailWidgetDeepLink`, which lands on the controls that already work.
- Keep persisted identifiers stable: provider IDs, `SettingsKey` strings, `CloudSyncCoordinator.containerIdentifier`, `SharedStore.appGroupID`, widget kind, cache-key shape, and deep-link format are shared across launches, devices or targets. Update all entitlements/consumers together if an App Group or CloudKit container contract changes. The mirrored CloudKit schema is append-only once shipped, so a column added to `Hike` can never later change type or go away.
- Both unit-test bundles are hosted by the app, so it launches and runs its `.task`s before any test does. Startup work that writes shared state — today `OpenHikesView.restoreLastSelectedHike()`, which publishes a widget payload — must stay behind the `isRunningTests` guard, or it races the suites that assert on that state. The same guard is what keeps the test host from mirroring to the developer's real iCloud account, since it builds its own container at launch. UI tests run out-of-process and identify the app-under-test with `--ui-testing`. `Fixture.hike(in:configure:)` inserts before it runs `configure`, and must keep doing so: `Hike`'s device-local passthroughs are a silent no-op on a row with no `modelContext`.
- The app ships for iPhone only: every target declares `SUPPORTED_PLATFORMS = "iphoneos iphonesimulator"` and `TARGETED_DEVICE_FAMILY = 1`. An embedded extension's device family has to stay a subset of its host's, so `OpenWidget` moves with the app rather than independently. The `canImport(UIKit)`/`canImport(AppKit)` aliases and `#if os(iOS)` guards in the existing sources are kept — they cost nothing and are what a later iPad, Mac or visionOS target would be rebuilt from — but nothing verifies those paths compile any more, so treat them as unbuilt rather than supported.
- A composite row is one accessibility element, not four. `HikeRow`, `StatTile`, `DetailRow` and the settings rows hide their decoration and expose a single label/value pair, so a UI test locates a row by its identifier plus a label prefix (`hikeRow(titled:)` in `UITestSupport.swift`) rather than by the `staticTexts` inside it. Selection that is drawn only as a tint or a checkmark also carries `.isSelected`; a glyph-only button carries its own `accessibilityLabel` and a `minimumTapTarget()`. Anything decorative is `.accessibilityHidden(true)`, and a `Text` that interpolates an SF Symbol needs a spoken label beside it. An identifier on a container is worse than none: SwiftUI pushes it down onto every descendant, so it both smothers the leaf identifiers underneath it and makes a whole section answer to one name — which is why the surface and difficulty sections carry theirs on the bar alone. `AccessibilityUITests` and `AccessibilityLabelUITests` are what enforce this.
- `OpenHikes/PrivacyInfo.xcprivacy` is part of the shipping contract, not documentation. It declares four required-reason API codes — `CA92.1` for the app's own `UserDefaults`, `C617.1` and `3B52.1` for file timestamps inside the app's containers and through the document picker, and `35F9.1` for system uptime used as an elapsed-time measurement — plus `NSPrivacyTracking: false` and empty collected-data and tracking-domain arrays. An upload without it is rejected with ITMS-91053, and the rejection names the API rather than the manifest, so reaching for a new required-reason API means adding its code here in the same change. `OpenHikes/` is a file-system-synchronized group whose only membership exception is `Info.plist`, so the manifest is bundled with no `project.pbxproj` edit. Apple's authoritative code list is the DocC JSON behind `NSPrivacyAccessedAPITypeReasons`; the rendered HTML page is JavaScript-only and cannot be read by a fetch. `OpenWidgetExtension` deliberately carries **no** manifest of its own: it was audited and calls none of the required-reason APIs — `SharedStore` enumerates with `includingPropertiesForKeys: nil` and reads no timestamp, and the widget touches no `UserDefaults` and no uptime — so a manifest there would declare reasons the binary does not use. If a future upload rejection names the extension, that audit is what changed.
- `Info.plist` declares `NSSupportsLiveActivities`, without which `Activity.request` throws and nothing appears — the failure is silent from the walker's side. `NSSupportsLiveActivitiesFrequentUpdates` is deliberately *absent*: this app updates on the walker's own movement at a 20-second floor, which is well inside the ordinary budget, and asking for the frequent-update allowance would trade a battery warning in Settings for a rate nothing here wants. The walker's own switch is `SettingsKey.liveActivitiesEnabled`, on by default; the system's per-app switch is read separately through `areActivitiesEnabled`, and both have to say yes.
- Never commit `OpenHikes/Secrets.plist`. Copy `Secrets.example.plist` locally for Stadia or Thunderforest keys; OpenStreetMap remains the keyless default.

## Render isolation, in practice

The claim these rules protect is measured rather than asserted: an idle app with a map on screen evaluates zero SwiftUI bodies and costs 0.6% of one core, a sustained chart scrub moves the map seventeen times without re-evaluating any body above the chart, and a backgrounded recording renders nothing at all. `PERFORMANCE.md` carries the current numbers. Four rules below each produced a convincing wrong answer first, and are worth knowing before changing anything on the render path.

**Only a `View` type is a boundary.** A helper `func`, a computed `var`, and a `.toolbar`/`.safeAreaInset`/`.overlay` closure are all inlined into the body that declares them, so an observable read inside one registers as an input of *that* body. This is how a tick mark came to rebuild a whole photo grid: the selection lived correctly in an `@Observable` controller, and the cells were built by a `private func cell(_:at:)` in the sheet's scope. If a body is re-running and the observable read is not visible in it, look for those four before looking anywhere else.

**State can be correctly owned and incorrectly placed.** `@State` invalidates its declaring view whether or not `body` reads it — a navigation path held as `@State` on the root re-rendered the entire map screen underneath a full-screen cover that completely obscured it, and an `.onChange` writing a `@State` that no body ever read still cost two body evaluations. `SheetPresentation` is the fix shape: a stable `@Observable` holding the raw state as `@ObservationIgnored` storage and publishing only coarser derived flags, so pushing a photo onto a hike — the same screen at the same height — flips nothing at all.

**A computed property that sorts looks like a field access.** `Hike.orderedPhotos` was read six times in one body pass of the photo viewer for that reason. Its comparator also allocated: comparing `(capturedAt, id.uuidString)` tuples makes Swift build both sides before comparing, so every comparison allocated two 36-character strings rather than only the ties the tie-break exists for.

**Not every well-argued prediction survives a measurement.** `SettingsView`'s unbounded `@Query` was predicted to charge all seven `Form` sections for every write to any `Hike`. Measured, it was 2.0 body evaluations either way, because SwiftData coalesces the writes into one invalidation the explicit state changes already paid for. A prediction about SwiftUI cost is a hypothesis; measure both sides.

**A same-value write is filtered by `@Observable`, not by SwiftData — and only when the type is `Equatable`.** Measured across `String`, `Double`, `Bool`, `Date`, `UUID`, `String?`, dictionaries, an `@Attribute(.externalStorage)` array and a to-many relationship: a `@Model` notifies on **every** write, equal or not, inserted into a context or not, and does so per-property. A plain `@Observable` storing an `Equatable` value notifies on **none** of them; storing a non-`Equatable` one — `CLLocationCoordinate2D` — notifies on all. The filtering lives in `@Observable`'s macro expansion. Three consequences. A dedup guard on an `Equatable` `@Observable` property (`RouteStyle.apply`, `SheetPresentation.pathDidChange`) is belt-and-braces over undocumented runtime behaviour and **cannot be protected by a zero-assertion test** — delete it and the test stays green, because the runtime already filtered the write. A dedup guard on a non-`Equatable` one (`RouteHighlight.move(to:)`, `LocationManager.publish`) is load-bearing app code and its test really does go red. And a test asserting a zero *upstream* of an `@Observable` needs an explicit precondition that the write it is filtering actually happened, or it measures nothing. `OpenHikesTests/Map/RenderIsolationTests+Observation.swift` pins both runtime behaviours; those pins are the tripwire if either changes, and they are the one thing in that family that cannot be mutation-verified, since a runtime change cannot be induced.

**A zero-assertion is only evidence if you have watched it go red.** Around thirty in the render-isolation family were audited by deleting the behaviour each claimed to hold; two were decorative for the reason above, and one hole was real and unrelated — `LocationManager.minimumPublishInterval` could be deleted entirely with the whole suite still green, because `ObservationCounter` re-arms through a `Task` and so sees ten writes in one runloop turn exactly once either way. An observation count cannot measure a throttle; assert the throttle's observable effect instead.

Use `RenderSignpost` and the `RENDER_SIGNPOST_LOG=1` scheme variable when changing this flow, and add a mark for any new work placed on the path — `Purchases/` and the widget's timeline provider carry none today, which is precisely why a rendering problem in either would be invisible to the performance suite.

## Maintaining the performance harness

Every rule here produced a convincing wrong answer first, and each one is a way for `PerformanceUITests` to report a number that is about the harness rather than the app.

**The observer perturbs the observed.** The first interaction with a newly-presented screen forces XCUITest to hit-test against a hierarchy it has not described before, and SwiftUI evaluates bodies to answer — charged to the gesture, this made one chart scrub report 2 and 5 on consecutive runs of identical code. `warmAccessibilityTree(around:in:)` pays that cost before the baseline reading, but it performs a real centre tap and so has to be *aimed*: warming on the photo strip navigates into the viewer, and warming on the Settings form's centre lands on the tile-provider list and either switches the map source or opens the paywall. Warm on a harmless control on the same screen, after scrolling it into view.

**A fixed settle time cannot be both correct and fast.** `settle(in:)` polls the app's own counters and returns once nothing has re-rendered for 1.5 s, ignoring the sampler's entries — which tick every second regardless and would otherwise mean the app never looked quiet. A new counter that ticks on a timer **must** be added to the `sampled` exclusion set in `PerformanceCounters.isEquivalent(to:)`, or every recording scenario spins to its timeout.

**A suite made entirely of upper bounds cannot notice work that has stopped.** Instrumenting the 1 Hz clock nearly broke it: extracting the readout into a view that stored the *recorder* made the view structurally identical on every tick, so SwiftUI skipped its body and the clock silently froze — scoring perfectly against every budget in the suite. The view now stores the formatted string, so what SwiftUI diffs is the thing on screen, and `RecordingClockTick` carries a *lower* bound in the foreground scenario as well as an upper bound in the backgrounded one. Any counter measuring work that is supposed to happen needs the same pair.

**A cache is a lie detector that has already been bribed.** The offline scenario asserts that browsing opens no connection, and on its first run it passed instantly and proved nothing — every tile in the region was already on disk from the previous scenario, so there was no miss and no fetch to refuse. `--ui-test-offline` hands the launch an empty tile root for this reason, which turned 0 refusals into 45.

**A permission dialog must not decide whether you get data.** The recording scenario once reset location authorization and relied on a UI interruption monitor to answer the alert; when that failed, Core Location delivered nothing and the run produced fifty-one seconds of an idle app, which looks like a measurement but is the absence of one. `Scripts/run-performance-tests.sh` grants the permission out-of-band with `simctl privacy`, and the monitor stays only as a fallback.

**A harness failure will happily impersonate a product failure.** Four runs back to back once produced a different failure each time — `kAXErrorServerNotFound`, `Error getting main window`, `Application … is not running` — and never the same test twice. None were assertions; all were the accessibility server being asked about an app that had not finished coming forward, because both `launch()` and `activate()` return before the state they name is true. `bringToForeground(_:)` blocks on `XCUIApplication.wait(for: .runningForeground)` first. When a performance suite starts failing *differently* on each run, suspect the harness.

**A test the runner cannot find is a test that passes.** `run-performance-tests.sh` once built its list by scanning `PerformanceUITests.swift` alone, after the suite had grown into `+Photos.swift` and `+Screens.swift`, so `--list` under-reported and `--test` rejected names that existed. It scans `PerformanceUITests*.swift` now. Anything that decides *which* tests run is part of the harness and needs the same suspicion as the assertions.

**A ratio can invent a finding.** The report generator once flagged a backgrounded recording for "52.2 network requests per accepted fix", which was arithmetic rather than a fact: it charged the tiles the foreground map loaded at launch against the three fixes a short scenario accepts. That scenario in fact woke the radio zero times. The generator counts requests inside the backgrounded windows now.

There is no canonical list of signpost names, and any list written into a document would drift: `RenderSignpost` takes a `StaticString`, so a name exists only at its call site. Read them off the code instead — `rg -o --no-filename 'RenderSignpost\.\w+\(\s*"[A-Za-z]+"' --glob '*.swift' | sed -E 's/.*"([A-Za-z]+)".*/\1/' | sort -u`. The prefixes worth knowing are `…Body` for a SwiftUI body evaluation, `Map…` for anything reaching `MKMapView`, `Recording…`/`Live…` for the fix pipeline — with `LiveActivity…` the exception, which is the Lock Screen panel rather than a fix —, `Photo…` for decode and ordering, `Tile…`/`Offline…` for storage and download, and `AppModelInit`/`ModelContainerInit`/`GPXParsed`/`HikeTrailAnalysis` for startup and I/O intervals.

`General/Diagnostics/FieldMetrics/` is the MetricKit half, and note it is *not* `#if DEBUG` — unlike everything else in `Diagnostics/` — because MetricKit only delivers against Release builds in the field. It is split along one line: `FieldMetricsDigest.swift` holds every judgement the app makes about a payload and imports no MetricKit at all, which is the only reason `FieldMetricsDigestTests` can exist, since `MXMetricPayload` has no initializer and cannot be synthesised. Only four `mxSignpost` spans exist, deliberately: Apple limits how many the system processes and the failure mode is silent, so a fifth span does not error, it costs the other four their data. `FieldSignpost.Span` is `CaseIterable` and its count is asserted, so a fifth has to be added on purpose.

## Energy policies in force

Three policies decide what the app spends. Each was a measured finding once and each is now shipping behaviour, with the full argument in the source header so the rationale cannot drift away from the code it justifies. Do not weaken one without a measurement.

- **GPS accuracy is a function of conditions**, not a constant (`Recording/RecordingEnergyPolicy.swift`). `desiredAccuracy` drops only for Low Power Mode or thermal `.serious` and above; `distanceFilter` widens for those and for standing still, taking the larger candidate. `.fair` thermal is deliberately excluded — a phone in a sunlit jacket pocket sits there all summer, and a mitigation that is always on is indistinguishable from having lowered the default. `PowerStateMonitor` watches both notifications, so the transition with no fix to prompt it — a walker stopping for lunch as the battery crosses 20% — still reconfigures.
- **Tile fetching is split by purpose**, not by caller (`Tiles/TileNetworkPolicy.swift`). What matters is whether anyone is waiting for the tile: `loadTile` takes the purpose and defaults to `.interactive`, while `saveTileDurably` fixes it at `.speculative`. Cellular allows interactive and denies speculative; offline and Low Data Mode deny both; Low Power Mode and thermal pressure deny only speculative. The asymmetry is the point — a walker looking at the map gets their tile, and what stops is the app spending a metered radio on tiles nobody asked to see. None of it is configurable, because a switch is a question the walker has to answer correctly *before* the walk to get the right behaviour during it. Every refusal emits `TileFetchSuppressed` with `purpose=` and `reason=`; a tile that silently never loads is the hardest thing in this pipeline to debug, and this policy creates that situation on purpose.
- **A backgrounded recording draws nothing and ticks nothing.** `MapView.Coordinator` gates the overlay apply on foreground, observed through `UIApplication` lifecycle notifications rather than `scenePhase` so it stays entirely off SwiftUI's render path; the `withObservationTracking` registration continues regardless, since the revision must keep being tracked, and the work is deferred rather than dropped and caught up in one pass on return. `RecordingHeader` builds its 1 Hz `TimelineView` only while `scenePhase` is `.active` — that one *is* on the render path, deliberately, because the question is whether the `TimelineView` is in the hierarchy at all and only SwiftUI can answer it. Do not assume iOS suspends that timer: a suspended app runs no timers, but this app holds the location background mode for the entire hike, which is exactly what keeps it running.

## Settled decisions — do not re-raise

Each of these looks like a finding and has already been investigated. Re-opening one needs new evidence, not a fresh reading of the same code.

**Types that should not become actors.** `TileCache`, whose `Mutex<MutationVersions>` makes bump-then-delete atomic against check-then-write whereas an actor's suspension points reintroduce the interleavings it exists to forbid. `HikePhotoStore`, whose only mutable state is an already-thread-safe `NSCache`, and where an actor would serialise thumbnail decodes that today run in parallel across gallery tiles. `SerialAsyncQueue`, because an actor gives mutual exclusion but explicitly not FIFO ordering across suspensions, and offers no barrier — both of which the "every fix accepted before now is on disk once the queue drains" invariant depends on. `SharedStore`, whose hazard is cross-process and therefore beyond in-process isolation; `options: .atomic` is the right answer and is used on every write. `RecordingStats` and `RecordingTrace`, read synchronously by `MapView.Coordinator` inside `withObservationTracking`, where isolation would put an `await` in the MapKit render path. And `PendingRecordingFixStore.withExclusiveLock`, whose `flock()` is cross-process and cannot be expressed by an actor.

**Older API that is justified, not legacy.** `MKMapView` behind `UIViewRepresentable` rather than SwiftUI `Map`: `Map` re-diffs its content builder on every `@Observable` change, which is the exact cost render isolation exists to avoid, and there is no SwiftUI equivalent for `MKUserTrackingButton` or for the `CachingTileOverlayRenderer` and `DirectionalPolylineRenderer` subclasses. `CLLocationManager` and its delegate rather than `CLLocationUpdate.liveUpdates()`, which stalls after the first fix when the Simulator is driven by `simctl location … start`. The six remaining GCD uses, each required by an API with no async form or by synchronous blocking work that should not be awaited — this is not a codebase that reached for GCD out of habit, since `Synchronization.Mutex` and `Atomic` appear across 17 files. `UIImagePickerController` for camera capture, whose camera source is not deprecated but is the system camera. The force unwraps of string-literal `URL(string:)` in `MapPurchaseLinks` and `TileAttribution`, wrapped in explicit lint pragmas. The `fatalError` in `OpenHikesModel` for a data store that cannot be created. And the 128 `canImport(UIKit)`/`#if os(iOS)` guards across 37 files, kept as the basis for a later platform target — unbuilt, not supported.

**A store-open failure is reported without attribution, on purpose.** Both the mirrored `Hike` store and the unmirrored `HikeLocalState` store are configurations of one `ModelContainer`, so a corrupt sidecar fails the open exactly as hard as a corrupt primary, and `StorageStartupIssue` carries only `underlyingDescription` — the two arrive as the same string. `loadContainer` catches, falls back to in-memory and raises the alert; the `fatalError` in `loadDefaultContainer` fires only if the in-memory fallback also fails, which is not a user-reachable path. Attributing the failure to one store would need a second store-open on the launch path to produce a message the user cannot act on, since the answer to both is the same reinstall. `StorageStartupTests.failuresAreIndistinguishable` pins this so it reads as a decision rather than an oversight.

**Deliberate test seams, not production indirection.** The injectable transports, clocks, defaults, location sources and containers on `OverpassTrailGraphProvider`, `BackgroundTrailTracker`, `OfflineTileDownloader`, `CloudSyncCoordinator`, `LocationManager`, `MapEntitlementStore` and `TileSandbox` exist so suites never touch the app's singletons, the network or wall-clock time. That isolation did not go away with test parallelism: the whole bundle runs in one process, so a suite reaching for `TileCache.shared` would still leak into the next one. The photo domain's ten small types are the same story — every one is under 250 lines with a single responsibility, and several exist because PhotoKit cannot be tested without a protocol seam. No collapse is recommended for either.

**Environment capabilities that are absent, not missing.** `StoreKitTest` cannot be used in this project, and the finding is the constraint rather than the suite. It needs a warnings-as-errors exemption merely to compile — Apple's own `SKTestTransaction.h` declares an `SKPaymentTransactionState` deprecated in iOS 18, and `SWIFT_TREAT_WARNINGS_AS_ERRORS` reaches the Clang module build, so the `.pcm` fails to emit and nothing in the bundle compiles. `OTHER_SWIFT_FLAGS = "$(inherited) -Xcc -Wno-error=deprecated-declarations"` on `OpenHikesTests` does fix that, and buys nothing: with the flag applied, `SKTestSession` still does not attach to `storekitd` under `xcodebuild test` on Xcode 26.6 / iOS 26.5. The session constructs, then `storefront` is empty rather than the `USA` in `OpenHikes.storekit`, `Product.products(for:)` returns nothing, `buyProduct` throws `notEntitled`, and storekitd logs the app talking to the *Sandbox* server — because the `.storekit` configuration is synced to the device by the Xcode IDE and not by the command line. App entitlements, stale daemon state and a `<StoreKitConfigurationFileReference>` in the scheme's TestAction were each ruled out by measurement. Separately, `AppStore.sync()` — which `restore()` is built on — never returns in a hosted unit test, observed past ten minutes, so a `restore()` test would hang the bundle rather than fail it. `MapEntitlementStoreLaunchTests`' header carries the whole argument; what *is* reachable is covered through the existing injectable seams.

**Claims investigated and found false.** The widget deep link does not need a `CFBundleURLTypes` registration; the system routes a `widgetURL` straight to the owning app, as `TrailWidgetDeepLink.swift` documents, so the scheme is only a label. A trim cannot delete a tile a concurrent auto-save just promoted: `trimCache` skips claimed names outright, and a tile promoted after the claim snapshot keeps its fetch-time mtime and so sorts last in the oldest-first deletion order. `RouteMotion` really is written by `RecordingPoint.routeCoordinate` and read by nothing but tests — the call sites that appear to read it read `RecordingMotionState` and `RecordingPointFlags.nonPedestrian`, which are different types. Syncing `tileProviderID` does not leave a keyless device with a blank map, because `TileProvider.renderable(id:)` falls back to the keyless default and `SettingsView.providerRow` compares against that effective provider. `Color+Hex` existing in both the app and the shared package is the ordinary cost of a widget target that cannot import the app, and `ColorHexTests` asserts parity between the two. And `PhotoLibraryReader` asking for `.readWrite` is correct rather than over-broad: `.addOnly` cannot read assets, and `.readWrite` is the only level that supports the limited-access flow. The bare `Task {}` calls on `@MainActor` types are not violations of the rule above: every one of them *is* main-actor work — a journal flush timer, a widget-fix merge into a `@MainActor` method, an `Observations` loop that calls `updateEnergyProfile()`, a hop into the `TrailBasemapRenderer` actor, a prefetch that then writes main-actor state — and the flagship example, `HikePhotoImport.discardFiles` reaching `erase()`, is already off-main because `HikePhotoStore.remove` calls `assertOffMainThread`. `Task.detached` would not even be the fix there: strip `@concurrent` from `erase()` and the callee becomes `@MainActor`, so the detached task hops straight back. The escape is `@concurrent` or `nonisolated` on the *callee*, which is what `scheduleLiveMatching` relies on. And `aps-environment = development` in `OpenHikes.entitlements` is correct in the tree: `CODE_SIGN_STYLE` is `Automatic`, so Xcode substitutes `production` on archive, and `development` is what a local build needs to register for push at all.

**ActivityKit's own shape, worked around rather than fought.** `Activity<Attributes>` is a plain **non-Sendable class** whose `update` and `end` are `nonisolated async`, so holding one on a `@MainActor` type and awaiting a method on it is a region-isolation error — `SystemHikeActivityPresenter` boxes it in a `private nonisolated struct Handle: @unchecked Sendable` and crosses through two `nonisolated static` functions. The `nonisolated` on the box is load-bearing: `SWIFT_DEFAULT_ACTOR_ISOLATION = MainActor` would otherwise make the box itself main-actor isolated and the property unable to leave. `ActivityState` gained a `.pending` case in iOS 26, and with warnings as errors a non-exhaustive switch fails the build, so `isLive` names `.pending`, `.active` and `.stale` positively rather than defaulting. And the presenter *adopts* an already-running activity rather than requesting a second, because the system restores activities across a relaunch and a second request would leave two panels for one walk.

**ActivityKit cannot be exercised from a hosted unit test.** Under `xcodebuild test`, `ActivityAuthorizationInfo` reports activities disabled and `Activity.request` throws; nothing makes either say otherwise, so a suite talking to the framework could only assert that nothing happened. Everything worth asserting is policy and sits above the `HikeActivityPresenting` seam, where `StubHikeActivityPresenter` watches it — which is also why `OpenHikesModel.makeLiveActivityController(defaults:)` returns `nil` under `AppLaunchEnvironment.isHostingTests` and the recorder and tracker both take the controller as an optional. UI tests, which run out of process, keep theirs.

**Assumptions that are load-bearing but unobserved.** MapKit is assumed to re-enter `draw` after every `setNeedsDisplay(_ mapRect:)` and to be the only thing that invalidates a tile; the whole overzoom path rests on both, and the redraw loop `CachingTileOverlayRenderer.fetchPath(drawing:maximumZ:isCached:)` closes was reasoned about rather than observed under Instruments, as was the blank sibling that closing it exposed. `@Attribute(.externalStorage)` on `Hike.route` and `Hike.rawRoute` is assumed to be what makes mirroring carry them as a `CKAsset` rather than a record field — documented behaviour that compiles, but nothing here has watched a twenty-thousand-point route cross a real container.

## Documentation

Four files with distinct jobs. Keep a fact in exactly one of them.

- `README.md` is for someone who just found the repository: what the app is, what it needs, how to build and run it, and how it is laid out. Engineering rationale does not belong there.
- `.github/copilot-instructions.md` — this file — holds the durable conventions, commands, architecture rules and settled decisions.
- `CODE_REVIEW.md` and `PERFORMANCE.md` are **live lists, not logs**. A finding that has been fixed is deleted rather than annotated, and a claim that stopped matching the code is deleted whether or not anything was done about it. Neither is a changelog; git already is one.

Cite these documents from source comments by *section name*, never by finding number or quoted figure. Numbered citations went stale within a single revision — comments referring to "Finding 1" and "Finding 2" survived the findings being renumbered, and quoted millisecond figures the documents no longer contained.
